COSMOLOGY
Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe.
Modern cosmology combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy.
The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy.
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old according to current measurements.
The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while light was traveling.
The observable universe is the region from which light or other signals have had time to reach us.
The entire universe may be much larger than the observable universe.
Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite is not currently known.

## OBSERVATIONAL COSMOLOGY

Observational cosmology uses astronomical measurements to test models of the universe.
The cosmic microwave background is one of its most important datasets.
Type Ia supernovae are used as distance indicators for studying cosmic expansion.
Galaxy surveys measure positions, redshifts, and properties of millions of galaxies.
Baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler for measuring cosmic distances.
Weak gravitational lensing traces the distribution of matter.
Galaxy clusters provide information about structure growth and dark matter.

## COSMOLOGICAL DISTANCES

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.
Comoving distance accounts for cosmic expansion when describing large-scale positions.
Proper distance describes physical separation at a specified cosmic time.
Lookback time measures how long light has traveled to reach an observer.
Luminosity distance is defined using the observed brightness of an object.
Angular-diameter distance relates an object's physical size to its observed angular size.

## COSMOLOGICAL PRINCIPLE

The cosmological principle states that the universe is approximately homogeneous and isotropic on sufficiently large scales.
Homogeneous means that matter is statistically distributed similarly from place to place.
Isotropic means that the universe looks statistically similar in different directions.
The principle does not require galaxies to be uniformly distributed on small scales.
Galaxies form clusters, filaments, and voids on smaller scales.
Homogeneity becomes a useful approximation only over sufficiently large distances.
Observations of large-scale galaxy distributions support approximate large-scale homogeneity.
The cosmological principle is a foundational assumption in many cosmological models.
It simplifies the mathematical description of the expanding

The expansion rate also affects estimates of cosmic distances and ages.
Different cosmological parameters are strongly connected in cosmological models.

## COSMIC TIME

Looking farther into space generally means looking farther back in time.
Light requires a finite amount of time to travel between astronomical objects.
A galaxy millions of light-years away is observed as it existed millions of years ago.
Very distant galaxies are observed as they existed billions of years in the past.
The cosmic microwave background comes from an even earlier period.
Astronomers use distant observations to reconstruct the history of the universe.
Different wavelengths reveal different stages of cosmic evolution.
The expansion of space changes the wavelength of traveling light.
Cosmological distance and lookback time are related but are not identical quantities.
Cosmic history is therefore encoded in the light reaching Earth.

## Cosmological observations provide indirect constraints on early-universe physics.

Inflation can explain why widely separated regions of the observable universe have similar large-scale properties.
It can also explain why the observable universe appears close to spatially flat.
Quantum fluctuations during inflation can become seeds for later cosmic structure.
These fluctuations can be stretched to enormous scales during rapid expansion.
Inflation is supported indirectly by several features of observed cosmological structure.
The specific physical mechanism responsible for inflation has not been established.

## GEOMETRY OF THE UNIVERSE

The geometry of the universe describes its large-scale spatial curvature.
A universe can have positive, zero, or negative spatial curvature.
Positive curvature corresponds to a closed geometry in simple cosmological models.
Zero curvature corresponds to a spatially flat geometry.
Negative curvature corresponds to an open geometry.

Cosmic geometry depends on the balance of matter, radiation, dark energy, and curvature.

The geometry of spacetime also includes time and is described by general relativity.

The cosmic microwave background is electromagnetic radiation left over from the early universe.
It was released when the universe became cool enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into neutral atoms.
This transition is called recombination.
The cosmic microwave background was emitted roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
The radiation has been stretched by cosmic expansion into microwave wavelengths.
Its present temperature is approximately 2.7 kelvin.
The CMB is observed across the entire sky with remarkable uniformity.
Tiny temperature fluctuations in the CMB contain information about early density variations.
These fluctuations later grew through gravity into galaxies and larger structures.

## CMB ANISOTROPIES

CMB anisotropies are small variations in the temperature of the cosmic microwave background.
These variations are typically measured at the level of tens of microkelvin.
They reflect differences in density and gravitational potential in the early universe.
The angular pattern of CMB fluctuations contains information about cosmological parameters.
Features in the CMB power spectrum reveal information about matter, radiation, and geometry.
The positions of acoustic peaks provide constraints on the composition and evolution of the universe.

## COSMIC STRUCTURE

The universe is organized into structures including galaxies, groups, clusters, filaments, and voids.
These structures form part of a large-scale pattern called the cosmic web.
Dark matter provides much of the gravitational framework for this structure.
Ordinary matter falls into dark-matter-dominated gravitational wells.
Gas cools and can form stars inside galaxies.
Galaxy groups and clusters form in regions where matter is especially concentrated.
Filaments connect dense regions across the cosmic web.
Voids contain relatively few galaxies compared with surrounding regions.
Structure formation is driven mainly by gravitational growth of initial density fluctuations.
The distribution of galaxies provides information about the underlying matter distribution.

## GALAXY REDSHIFT

Galaxy redshift describes the shift of spectral features toward longer wavelengths.
Cosmological redshift occurs because space expands as light travels through the universe.
For sufficiently distant galaxies, redshift is related to cosmic expansion.
Redshift can be measured from known spectral lines.
Astronomers use redshift to estimate distances and study the history of cosmic expansion.
Higher redshift generally corresponds to observing galaxies at earlier cosmic times.
Very distant galaxies are therefore seen as they existed billions of years ago.
Galaxy surveys use redshift to construct three-dimensional maps of cosmic structure.
Redshift is different from ordinary Doppler shifts caused solely by local motion.

## COSMIC WEB

The cosmic web is the large-scale network of matter throughout the universe.
It contains filaments, galaxy clusters, galaxy groups, and vast underdense voids.
Dark matter forms much of the underlying structure of the cosmic web.
Galaxies tend to trace the denser regions of this structure.
Filaments can contain gas and many galaxies.
Clusters often form where multiple filaments intersect.
Voids can span tens to hundreds of millions of light-years.
The cosmic web developed gradually through gravitational instability.
Large-scale galaxy surveys are used to map the cosmic web.

The Hubble constant describes the current rate of cosmic expansion.

Local distance-ladder measurements generally infer a higher expansion rate than some early-universe measurements.
This discrepancy is known as the Hubble tension.
The Hubble tension remains an active area of cosmological research.
Possible explanations include systematic measurement effects or new physics.
The Hubble constant is a fundamental parameter in modern cosmology.
Accurate distance measurements are important for determining the expansion rate.

Its gravitational effects reveal its presence around galaxies.
Dark-matter halos provide gravitational wells that help galaxies assemble.
The amount of dark matter strongly affects galaxy rotation.
Gravitational lensing can independently reveal dark-matter distributions.
Galaxy clusters contain large quantities of dark matter.
The nature of dark matter remains an open question in particle physics and cosmology.
Dark matter is different from ordinary gas, dust, stars, and planets.

This imbalance is called the matter-antimatter asymmetry.
The physical process that generated this asymmetry is not completely understood.

## ASTEROIDS — OVERVIEW

Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun.
Most asteroids are much smaller than planets.
Asteroids are remnants of material left over from the formation of the Solar System.
They are classified as small Solar System bodies.
Most known asteroids are concentrated in the main asteroid belt.
The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids can have irregular, spherical, elongated, or highly fractured shapes.
Their surfaces can contain rocks, dust, impact craters, and regolith.
Asteroids vary greatly in size, composition, brightness, and orbital properties.
Studying asteroids provides information about the early Solar System.

## FORMATION

Asteroids formed from material present in the protoplanetary disk.
The protoplanetary disk surrounded the young Sun.
Small solid particles collided and gradually accumulated during Solar System formation.
Gravitational interactions influenced how these bodies grew and moved.
In the asteroid belt, Jupiter's gravity prevented many objects from forming a single planet.
Collisions repeatedly fragmented larger bodies.
Some asteroids are therefore fragments of older parent bodies.
Other asteroids may preserve relatively primitive material.
Asteroids can retain chemical information from the early Solar System.

## Their compositions help scientists investigate planetary formation.

Asteroid formation and evolution occurred over billions of years.

## MAIN ASTEROID BELT

The main asteroid belt is located between Mars and Jupiter.
It extends roughly from 2.1 to 3.3 astronomical units from the Sun.
The asteroid belt is not a densely packed region of rocks.
Large distances separate most individual asteroids.
A spacecraft can travel through the asteroid belt without continuously encountering objects.
The total mass of the main asteroid belt is much less than Earth's mass.
Ceres is the largest object in the main asteroid belt.
Many smaller asteroids orbit throughout the region.
Orbital resonances with Jupiter create gaps in the asteroid belt.
These resonance gaps are known as Kirkwood gaps.
The asteroid belt contains diverse populations with different compositions.

## ASTEROID SIZE

Asteroids range from tiny fragments to bodies hundreds of kilometers across.
The largest asteroids are large enough to have approximately rounded shapes.
Smaller asteroids are often irregular because their gravity is weaker.
Ceres has a diameter of about 940 kilometers.
Vesta has a diameter of about 525 kilometers.
Many asteroids are only a few kilometers or less across.
Asteroid size affects gravity, surface shape, and geological evolution.
Larger asteroids can retain more internal heat.

## Smaller asteroids generally cool more rapidly after formation.

Asteroid sizes are commonly estimated using observations and physical models.

## COMPOSITION

Asteroids are made from different combinations of rock, metal, and carbon-rich material.

## Their compositions reflect different formation environments and histories.

Some asteroids contain large amounts of silicate minerals.
Some contain significant metallic iron and nickel.
Carbon-rich asteroids contain abundant carbon-bearing compounds.

Reflectance spectra can be used to classify asteroid types.

## ASTEROID TYPES

Asteroids are commonly grouped into broad spectral classes.
C-type asteroids are generally carbon-rich and relatively dark.
S-type asteroids are generally rich in silicate minerals.

## M-type asteroids are associated with metallic compositions.

Spectral classification is based partly on how asteroid surfaces reflect light.
Classification does not completely describe an asteroid's internal composition.
Spacecraft observations can provide more detailed information than remote spectroscopy.
Some asteroids do not fit neatly into a single traditional class.
Different asteroid populations are more common at different distances from the Sun.
Space weathering can alter the appearance of asteroid surfaces.
Taxonomic systems continue to be refined as observations improve.

## ORBITAL PROPERTIES

Asteroids orbit the Sun according to the laws of celestial mechanics.
Their orbits can be nearly circular or significantly elliptical.
Asteroid orbital inclination can vary widely.
Some asteroids have orbits that cross the paths of planets.
Gravitational encounters can change asteroid orbits over time.
Jupiter strongly influences the orbital evolution of many asteroids.
Planetary resonances can increase or decrease orbital stability.
Some asteroids become temporarily trapped in unusual orbital configurations.
Orbital calculations are used to predict future asteroid positions.
Long-term orbital prediction becomes more difficult when repeated gravitational encounters occur.

## NEAR-EARTH ASTEROIDS

Near-Earth asteroids are asteroids whose orbits bring them relatively close to Earth's orbit.
Their orbital paths can cross or approach Earth's orbital region.
Near-Earth objects are monitored because some could potentially impact Earth.
Most near-Earth asteroids do not pose an immediate threat.
Astronomers use repeated observations to improve their orbital calculations.
Radar observations can provide precise information about some nearby asteroids.
Space-based and ground-based telescopes contribute to asteroid surveys.
Impact probability depends on an object's orbit, size, and future trajectory.

## New observations can change calculated impact probabilities.

Monitoring improves the ability to identify potentially hazardous objects.

COSMOLOGY
Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe.
Modern cosmology combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy.
The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy.
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old according to current measurements.
The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while light was traveling.
The observable universe is the region from which light or other signals have had time to reach us.
The entire universe may be much larger than the observable universe.
Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite is not currently known.

Observational cosmology uses astronomical measurements to test models of the universe.
The cosmic microwave background is one of its most important datasets.
Type Ia supernovae are used as distance indicators for studying cosmic expansion.
Galaxy surveys measure positions, redshifts, and properties of millions of galaxies.
Baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler for measuring cosmic distances.
Weak gravitational lensing traces the distribution of matter.
Galaxy clusters provide information about structure growth and dark matter.

## HERTZSPRUNG-RUSSELL DIAGRAM

The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram compares stellar luminosity with surface temperature.
Temperature usually increases toward the left side of the diagram.
Luminosity generally increases upward.
Most stars lie along a diagonal region called the main sequence.
Red giants occupy a region above the main sequence.
White dwarfs are hot but relatively faint and occupy a lower-left region.
Supergiants occupy regions of very high luminosity.
The diagram is useful for studying stellar evolution.
A star's position changes as its temperature and luminosity change.
Clusters of stars can be studied using the diagram to estimate their ages.

## ASTEROIDS — OVERVIEW

Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun.
Most asteroids are much smaller than planets.
Asteroids are remnants of material left over from the formation of the Solar System.
They are classified as small Solar System bodies.
Most known asteroids are concentrated in the main asteroid belt.
The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids can have irregular, spherical, elongated, or highly fractured shapes.
Their surfaces can contain rocks, dust, impact craters, and regolith.
Asteroids vary greatly in size, composition, brightness, and orbital properties.
Studying asteroids provides information about the early Solar System.

## MAIN ASTEROID BELT

The main asteroid belt is located between Mars and Jupiter.
It extends roughly from 2.1 to 3.3 astronomical units from the Sun.
The asteroid belt is not a densely packed region of rocks.
Large distances separate most individual asteroids.
A spacecraft can travel through the asteroid belt without continuously encountering objects.
The total mass of the main asteroid belt is much less than Earth's mass.
Ceres is the largest object in the main asteroid belt.
Many smaller asteroids orbit throughout the region.
Orbital resonances with Jupiter create gaps in the asteroid belt.
These resonance gaps are known as Kirkwood gaps.
The asteroid belt contains diverse populations with different compositions.

Mission success is evaluated against predefined technical and scientific objectives.
A mission can remain scientifically valuable even if some secondary objectives fail.
Partial mission success can occur when only some instruments or mission phases operate as planned.
Unexpected discoveries can increase a mission's scientific importance.
Reliable data return is one of the most important measures of scientific mission performance.
Mission duration can exceed the original design lifetime when spacecraft systems remain healthy.
Extended missions can provide additional observations without requiring a new launch.
Mission operations must balance scientific opportunities against spacecraft safety.
Lessons from completed missions improve the design of future missions.

## PLANETS AND DWARF PLANETS

Planets and dwarf planets both orbit the Sun.
Both can have enough gravity to become approximately round.
The main difference is orbital dominance.
A planet has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.
A dwarf planet shares its orbital region with other objects.
Clearing an orbit does not mean removing every object from that region.
It refers to gravitational dominance over the surrounding orbital zone.
Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Neptune are examples of planets.
Ceres and Pluto are examples of dwarf planets.
The distinction is based on orbital dynamics rather than simply size.

## HERTZSPRUNG-RUSSELL DIAGRAM

The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram compares stellar luminosity with surface temperature.
Temperature usually increases toward the left side of the diagram.
Luminosity generally increases upward.
Most stars lie along a diagonal region called the main sequence.
Red giants occupy a region above the main sequence.
White dwarfs are hot but relatively faint and occupy a lower-left region.
Supergiants occupy regions of very high luminosity.
The diagram is useful for studying stellar evolution.
A star's position changes as its temperature and luminosity change.
Clusters of stars can be studied using the diagram to estimate their ages.

## ASTEROIDS — OVERVIEW

Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun.
Most asteroids are much smaller than planets.
Asteroids are remnants of material left over from the formation of the Solar System.
They are classified as small Solar System bodies.
Most known asteroids are concentrated in the main asteroid belt.
The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids can have irregular, spherical, elongated, or highly fractured shapes.
Their surfaces can contain rocks, dust, impact craters, and regolith.
Asteroids vary greatly in size, composition, brightness, and orbital properties.
Studying asteroids provides information about the early Solar System.

## MAIN ASTEROID BELT

The main asteroid belt is located between Mars and Jupiter.
It extends roughly from 2.1 to 3.3 astronomical units from the Sun.
The asteroid belt is not a densely packed region of rocks.
Large distances separate most individual asteroids.
A spacecraft can travel through the asteroid belt without continuously encountering objects.
The total mass of the main asteroid belt is much less than Earth's mass.
Ceres is the largest object in the main asteroid belt.
Many smaller asteroids orbit throughout the region.
Orbital resonances with Jupiter create gaps in the asteroid belt.
These resonance gaps are known as Kirkwood gaps.
The asteroid belt contains diverse populations with different compositions.

## MISSION SUCCESS

Mission success is evaluated against predefined technical and scientific objectives.
A mission can remain scientifically valuable even if some secondary objectives fail.
Partial mission success can occur when only some instruments or mission phases operate as planned.
Unexpected discoveries can increase a mission's scientific importance.
Reliable data return is one of the most important measures of scientific mission performance.
Mission duration can exceed the original design lifetime when spacecraft systems remain healthy.
Extended missions can provide additional observations without requiring a new launch.
Mission operations must balance scientific opportunities against spacecraft safety.
Lessons from completed missions improve the design of future missions.

## PLANETS AND DWARF PLANETS

Planets and dwarf planets both orbit the Sun.
Both can have enough gravity to become approximately round.
The main difference is orbital dominance.
A planet has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.
A dwarf planet shares its orbital region with other objects.
Clearing an orbit does not mean removing every object from that region.
It refers to gravitational dominance over the surrounding orbital zone.
Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Neptune are examples of planets.
Ceres and Pluto are examples of dwarf planets.
The distinction is based on orbital dynamics rather than simply size.

Neptune has an average density of about 1.64 grams per cubic centimeter.
Its blue appearance is influenced by methane in its atmosphere and atmospheric aerosols.

## GEOMETRY OF THE UNIVERSE

The geometry of the universe describes its large-scale spatial curvature.
A universe can have positive, zero, or negative spatial curvature.
Positive curvature corresponds to a closed geometry in simple cosmological models.
Zero curvature corresponds to a spatially flat geometry.
Negative curvature corresponds to an open geometry.
CMB observations indicate that the observable universe is very close to spatially flat.
Spatial flatness does not necessarily mean that the entire universe is finite or infinite.
Cosmic geometry depends on the balance of matter, radiation, dark energy, and curvature.
Measurements of the CMB and large-scale structure constrain spatial curvature.
The geometry of spacetime also includes time and is described by general relativity.

## Lambda-CDM successfully explains many observations across cosmic history.

It reproduces major features of the cosmic microwave background.
It explains the broad evolution of cosmic expansion.
The model contains several measured cosmological parameters.
Some observations, including the Hubble tension and the nature of dark energy, motivate tests beyond the basic model.

The universe is organized into structures including galaxies, groups, clusters, filaments, and voids.
These structures form part of a large-scale pattern called the cosmic web.
Dark matter provides much of the gravitational framework for this structure.
Ordinary matter falls into dark-matter-dominated gravitational wells.
Gas cools and can form stars inside galaxies.
Galaxy groups and clusters form in regions where matter is especially concentrated.
Filaments connect dense regions across the cosmic web.

Structure formation is driven mainly by gravitational growth of initial density fluctuations.
The distribution of galaxies provides information about the underlying matter distribution.

## COSMIC MICROWAVE BACKGROUND

The cosmic microwave background is electromagnetic radiation left over from the early universe.
It was released when the universe became cool enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into neutral atoms.
This transition is called recombination.
The cosmic microwave background was emitted roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
The radiation has been stretched by cosmic expansion into microwave wavelengths.
Its present temperature is approximately 2.7 kelvin.
The CMB is observed across the entire sky with remarkable uniformity.
Tiny temperature fluctuations in the CMB contain information about early density variations.
These fluctuations later grew through gravity into galaxies and larger structures.

COSMOLOGY
Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe.
Modern cosmology combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy.
The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy.
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old according to current measurements.

Observational cosmology uses astronomical measurements to test models of the universe.

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.

## COSMIC TIME

Looking farther into space generally means looking farther back in time.
Light requires a finite amount of time to travel between astronomical objects.
A galaxy millions of light-years away is observed as it existed millions of years ago.
Very distant galaxies are observed as they existed billions of years in the past.
The cosmic microwave background comes from an even earlier period.
Astronomers use distant observations to reconstruct the history of the universe.
Different wavelengths reveal different stages of cosmic evolution.
The expansion of space changes the wavelength of traveling light.
Cosmological distance and lookback time are related but are not identical quantities.
Cosmic history is therefore encoded in the light reaching Earth.

The principle does not require galaxies to be uniformly distributed on small scales.
Galaxies form clusters, filaments, and voids on smaller scales.
Homogeneity becomes a useful approximation only over sufficiently large distances.
Observations of large-scale galaxy distributions support approximate large-scale homogeneity.

Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe.
Modern cosmology combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy.
The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy.
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old according to current measurements.
The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while light was traveling.
The observable universe is the region from which light or other signals have had time to reach us.
The entire universe may be much larger than the observable universe.
Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite is not currently known.

## OBSERVATIONAL COSMOLOGY

Observational cosmology uses astronomical measurements to test models of the universe.
The cosmic microwave background is one of its most important datasets.
Type Ia supernovae are used as distance indicators for studying cosmic expansion.
Galaxy surveys measure positions, redshifts, and properties of millions of galaxies.
Baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler for measuring cosmic distances.
Weak gravitational lensing traces the distribution of matter.
Galaxy clusters provide information about structure growth and dark matter.

Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite is not currently known.
Cosmology studies the universe on scales much larger than individual galaxies.
The standard cosmological model is commonly called Lambda-CDM.

## DARK MATTER IN GALAXIES

Dark matter does not significantly interact with electromagnetic radiation.
It is therefore not directly visible through ordinary telescopes.
Its gravitational effects reveal its presence around galaxies.
Dark-matter halos provide gravitational wells that help galaxies assemble.
The amount of dark matter strongly affects galaxy rotation.
Gravitational lensing can independently reveal dark-matter distributions.
Galaxy clusters contain large quantities of dark matter.
The nature of dark matter remains an open question in particle physics and cosmology.
Dark matter is different from ordinary gas, dust, stars, and planets.
Understanding dark matter is essential for explaining the large-scale formation of galaxies.

Observational astronomy supports research into planetary systems, stellar evolution, galaxies, and cosmology.
Advances in detectors, telescopes, and data processing continue to increase the sensitivity of astronomical observations.
Modern astronomy increasingly combines observations from ground-based facilities, space observatories, and spacecraft.

Jupiter has a faint ring system.
The rings are much less prominent than Saturn's rings.
Jupiter's rings are composed mainly of fine dust particles.
Much of the ring material is believed to originate from impacts on small moons.
The main ring is surrounded by fainter ring structures.
Jupiter's rings are difficult to observe from Earth.
Spacecraft have provided detailed observations of the ring system.
The rings demonstrate that ring systems are not unique to Saturn.

## MAIN SEQUENCE

The main sequence is the longest major stage of a normal star's life.
During this stage, hydrogen is fused into helium in the core.
The Sun is currently a main-sequence star.
Main-sequence stars form a diagonal band on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
Massive main-sequence stars are generally hotter and more luminous.
Low-mass main-sequence stars are cooler and less luminous.
A star's main-sequence lifetime depends strongly on its mass.
Hydrogen gradually becomes depleted in the core.
When core hydrogen becomes insufficient, the star begins evolving away from the main sequence.

## ASTEROIDS — OVERVIEW

Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun.
Most asteroids are much smaller than planets.
Asteroids are remnants of material left over from the formation of the Solar System.
They are classified as small Solar System bodies.
Most known asteroids are concentrated in the main asteroid belt.
The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids can have irregular, spherical, elongated, or highly fractured shapes.
Their surfaces can contain rocks, dust, impact craters, and regolith.
Asteroids vary greatly in size, composition, brightness, and orbital properties.
Studying asteroids provides information about the early Solar System.

## MAIN ASTEROID BELT

The main asteroid belt is located between Mars and Jupiter.
It extends roughly from 2.1 to 3.3 astronomical units from the Sun.
The asteroid belt is not a densely packed region of rocks.
Large distances separate most individual asteroids.
A spacecraft can travel through the asteroid belt without continuously encountering objects.
The total mass of the main asteroid belt is much less than Earth's mass.
Ceres is the largest object in the main asteroid belt.
Many smaller asteroids orbit throughout the region.
Orbital resonances with Jupiter create gaps in the asteroid belt.
These resonance gaps are known as Kirkwood gaps.
The asteroid belt contains diverse populations with different compositions.

## HERTZSPRUNG-RUSSELL DIAGRAM

The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram compares stellar luminosity with surface temperature.
Temperature usually increases toward the left side of the diagram.
Luminosity generally increases upward.
Most stars lie along a diagonal region called the main sequence.
Red giants occupy a region above the main sequence.
White dwarfs are hot but relatively faint and occupy a lower-left region.
Supergiants occupy regions of very high luminosity.
The diagram is useful for studying stellar evolution.
A star's position changes as its temperature and luminosity change.
Clusters of stars can be studied using the diagram to estimate their ages.

Callisto: A heavily cratered outer Galilean moon.

Homogeneous means that matter is statistically distributed similarly from place to place.
Isotropic means that the universe looks statistically similar in different directions.
The principle does not require galaxies to be uniformly distributed on small scales.
Galaxies form clusters, filaments, and voids on smaller scales.
Homogeneity becomes a useful approximation only over sufficiently large distances.
Observations of large-scale galaxy distributions support approximate large-scale homogeneity.

## COSMIC VOID

A cosmic void is a large region of space containing relatively few galaxies.
Voids are not completely empty.
They can contain diffuse gas, dark matter, and isolated galaxies.
Matter tends to move away from underdense regions toward denser structures.
Voids therefore grow as surrounding matter becomes increasingly concentrated.
The size and distribution of voids depend on the growth of cosmic structure.
Void statistics can be used to test cosmological models.
Large-scale surveys identify voids from the distribution of galaxies.
Voids provide a complementary view of the cosmic web.

## COSMIC MICROWAVE BACKGROUND

The cosmic microwave background is electromagnetic radiation left over from the early universe.
It was released when the universe became cool enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into neutral atoms.
This transition is called recombination.
The cosmic microwave background was emitted roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
The radiation has been stretched by cosmic expansion into microwave wavelengths.
Its present temperature is approximately 2.7 kelvin.

## COSMIC WEB

The cosmic web is the large-scale network of matter throughout the universe.
It contains filaments, galaxy clusters, galaxy groups, and vast underdense voids.
Dark matter forms much of the underlying structure of the cosmic web.
Galaxies tend to trace the denser regions of this structure.
Filaments can contain gas and many galaxies.
Clusters often form where multiple filaments intersect.
Voids can span tens to hundreds of millions of light-years.
The cosmic web developed gradually through gravitational instability.
Large-scale galaxy surveys are used to map the cosmic web.

## COSMIC TIME

Looking farther into space generally means looking farther back in time.
Light requires a finite amount of time to travel between astronomical objects.
A galaxy millions of light-years away is observed as it existed millions of years ago.
Very distant galaxies are observed as they existed billions of years in the past.
The cosmic microwave background comes from an even earlier period.
Astronomers use distant observations to reconstruct the history of the universe.
Different wavelengths reveal different stages of cosmic evolution.
The expansion of space changes the wavelength of traveling light.
Cosmological distance and lookback time are related but are not identical quantities.
Cosmic history is therefore encoded in the light reaching Earth.

## COSMOLOGICAL DISTANCES

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.
Comoving distance accounts for cosmic expansion when describing large-scale positions.
Proper distance describes physical separation at a specified cosmic time.
Lookback time measures how long light has traveled to reach an observer.
Luminosity distance is defined using the observed brightness of an object.
Angular-diameter distance relates an object's physical size to its observed angular size.

The Big Bang model describes the universe evolving from an extremely hot, dense early state.
The model does not describe an explosion occurring at a single location in pre-existing space.
Instead, the expansion involves space itself changing with time.
The early universe was much hotter and denser than it is today.
As the universe expanded, its average temperature decreased.
Matter eventually formed atoms after the universe cooled sufficiently.
Later, gravity caused matter to gather into stars, galaxies, and larger structures.
The Big Bang model is supported by several independent observations.

## 13. INTERIOR

Venus is expected to have a metallic core.
A rocky mantle surrounds the core.
A rocky crust forms the outer solid layer.
The interior structure is broadly similar to that of Earth.

## 14. RING MOONS

Several moons orbit within or near Saturn's ring system.
Some small moons are called shepherd moons.
Shepherd moons can confine or shape narrow ring structures.
Prometheus and Pandora interact strongly with Saturn's F ring.
Pan and Daphnis occupy regions associated with gaps in the rings.
Moon-ring interactions create waves and disturbances.
The gravitational influence of moons helps maintain some ring features.
The rings and moons form an interconnected dynamical system.
Studying these interactions helps explain how planetary ring systems evolve.

## DARK MATTER

Dark matter is a form of matter inferred primarily through gravitational effects.
It does not emit, absorb, or reflect electromagnetic radiation strongly enough to be directly seen.
Galaxy rotation provides important evidence for dark matter.
Gravitational lensing provides additional evidence for its presence.
Galaxy clusters contain large amounts of dark matter.
Dark matter helps explain how cosmic structures form and grow.
Cold dark matter describes particles that moved relatively slowly when important structures formed.
The Lambda-CDM model assumes cold dark matter.
The identity of the dark-matter particle has not been established.

## 3. FORMATION

Jupiter formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago.
Jupiter formed from material in the early Solar System.
The planet formed in the colder outer region of the protoplanetary disk.
Hydrogen and helium were abundant in the early Solar System.
Jupiter accumulated a large amount of gas during its formation.
Its large mass allowed it to retain substantial hydrogen and helium.
The exact details of Jupiter's formation are still studied.
Models of Jupiter's formation help explain the structure of the Solar System.
Jupiter's composition provides evidence about conditions in the early planetary system.

## 8. INTERNAL STRUCTURE

Mercury has a large metallic core.
The core occupies a substantial fraction of Mercury's interior.
The core is surrounded by a rocky mantle.
A rocky crust forms the outermost solid layer.
Mercury's core contains a significant amount of iron.
The large core contributes to Mercury's relatively high average density.
Mercury has a global magnetic field.
The magnetic field provides evidence that at least part of the core remains active.
Scientists study Mercury's interior using spacecraft measurements and gravitational data.
Understanding Mercury's core helps explain how small terrestrial planets evolve.

## INTERNAL HEAT

Neptune emits more energy than it receives from sunlight.
The excess energy indicates that Neptune releases significant internal heat.
Internal heat can influence atmospheric circulation.
Heat from the interior may contribute to strong winds and storms.
The exact mechanism transporting internal heat remains an area of research.
Neptune's internal heat is important when comparing it with Uranus.
Both planets are ice giants with similar overall compositions.
Neptune produces substantially more internal energy than Uranus.
Differences in internal structure may help explain their different atmospheric behavior.
Studying internal heat helps scientists understand ice giant evolution.

## DWARF PLANETS AND ORBITAL DYNAMICS

Dwarf planets do not gravitationally dominate their orbital neighborhoods.
Their orbital regions contain many other small bodies.
Resonances can stabilize or modify their orbital paths.
Gravitational interactions can change orbital eccentricity and inclination.
Some dwarf planets have highly inclined or elongated orbits.
Orbital dynamics help explain the different populations of distant objects.
Long-term simulations are used to study their orbital evolution.
The gravitational influence of Neptune is particularly important beyond its orbit.
Close encounters can alter the trajectories of smaller bodies.
Orbital dynamics are central to understanding why dwarf planets differ from planets.

## ORBITAL MIGRATION

Planetary migration occurs when a planet's orbit changes after formation.
Interactions with a protoplanetary disk can alter orbital distance.
Gravitational interactions between planets can also change their orbits.
A planet can move closer to or farther from its host star.
Migration can explain planets found extremely close to their stars.
It can also influence the arrangement of multiple-planet systems.
Migration may occur during the early stages of planetary system evolution.
Resonances can develop when migrating planets interact gravitationally.
Planetary migration is an important part of modern planet-formation models.
The exact migration history of an individual exoplanet may be difficult to determine.

## ICE GIANT INTERIOR

The term ice giant refers to Uranus and Neptune.
In planetary science, "ice" includes substances such as water, ammonia, and methane.
These materials can exist in unusual high-pressure states inside a planet.
The deep interior of Uranus is extremely hot and highly compressed.
Water may become electrically conductive under extreme interior conditions.
Laboratory experiments study high-pressure water states relevant to ice giants.
Superionic water is one proposed state that may occur deep inside Uranus.
Such exotic states could help explain the planet's magnetic field.
Interior models are based on observations, physics, and computer simulations.
The exact internal structure of Uranus is not directly observable.

## 16. MAGNETIC FIELD AND ATMOSPHERIC LOSS

Mars does not currently have a strong global magnetic field like Earth.
Some regions of the Martian crust retain evidence of ancient magnetization.
This suggests Mars may have had a stronger global magnetic field early in its history.
The loss of a global magnetic field allowed the solar wind to interact more directly with the upper atmosphere.
Solar wind interactions can contribute to atmospheric escape.
Atmospheric loss is one factor in the long-term evolution of Mars.
Mars's thin present atmosphere may partly result from billions of years of atmospheric loss.
Studying atmospheric escape helps explain how Mars changed from its ancient environment to its present state.

## ASTEROIDS — OVERVIEW

Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun.
Most asteroids are much smaller than planets.
Asteroids are remnants of material left over from the formation of the Solar System.
They are classified as small Solar System bodies.
Most known asteroids are concentrated in the main asteroid belt.
The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids can have irregular, spherical, elongated, or highly fractured shapes.
Their surfaces can contain rocks, dust, impact craters, and regolith.
Asteroids vary greatly in size, composition, brightness, and orbital properties.
Studying asteroids provides information about the early Solar System.

## FORMATION

Asteroids formed from material present in the protoplanetary disk.
The protoplanetary disk surrounded the young Sun.
Small solid particles collided and gradually accumulated during Solar System formation.
Gravitational interactions influenced how these bodies grew and moved.
In the asteroid belt, Jupiter's gravity prevented many objects from forming a single planet.
Collisions repeatedly fragmented larger bodies.
Some asteroids are therefore fragments of older parent bodies.
Other asteroids may preserve relatively primitive material.
Asteroids can retain chemical information from the early Solar System.

The observed asymmetry is an important unresolved problem in fundamental physics.
Understanding baryogenesis could explain why ordinary matter exists in large quantities today.

INFLATION
Inflation is a proposed period of extremely rapid expansion in the very early universe.
Inflation can explain why widely separated regions of the observable universe have similar large-scale properties.
It can also explain why the observable universe appears close to spatially flat.
Quantum fluctuations during inflation can become seeds for later cosmic structure.
These fluctuations can be stretched to enormous scales during rapid expansion.
Inflation is supported indirectly by several features of observed cosmological structure.
The specific physical mechanism responsible for inflation has not been established.
Different inflationary models propose different fields and potential energy landscapes.

raw_bm25.text:
The Big Bang model is supported by several independent observations.
These include cosmic expansion, the cosmic microwave background, and the observed abundance of light elements.
The model describes the evolution of the observable universe but does not by itself explain every question about the ultimate beginning.

## 13. INTERIOR

Venus is expected to have a metallic core.
A rocky mantle surrounds the core.
A rocky crust forms the outer solid layer.
The interior structure is broadly similar to that of Earth.
The exact physical state of Venus's core is not completely known.
Scientists use gravity measurements and geological observations to study Venus's interior.
The planet's interior heat influences its geological activity.
Understanding the interior helps explain volcanism and tectonic deformation.

## 14. RING MOONS

Several moons orbit within or near Saturn's ring system.
Some small moons are called shepherd moons.
Shepherd moons can confine or shape narrow ring structures.
Prometheus and Pandora interact strongly with Saturn's F ring.
Pan and Daphnis occupy regions associated with gaps in the rings.
Moon-ring interactions create waves and disturbances.
The gravitational influence of moons helps maintain some ring features.
The rings and moons form an interconnected dynamical system.
Studying these interactions helps explain how planetary ring systems evolve.

## DARK MATTER

Dark matter is a form of matter inferred primarily through gravitational effects.
It does not emit, absorb, or reflect electromagnetic radiation strongly enough to be directly seen.
Galaxy rotation provides important evidence for dark matter.
Gravitational lensing provides additional evidence for its presence.
Galaxy clusters contain large amounts of dark matter.
Dark matter helps explain how cosmic structures form and grow.
Cold dark matter describes particles that moved relatively slowly when important structures formed.
The Lambda-CDM model assumes cold dark matter.
The identity of the dark-matter particle has not been established.

## 3. FORMATION

Jupiter formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago.
Jupiter formed from material in the early Solar System.
The planet formed in the colder outer region of the protoplanetary disk.
Hydrogen and helium were abundant in the early Solar System.
Jupiter accumulated a large amount of gas during its formation.
Its large mass allowed it to retain substantial hydrogen and helium.
The exact details of Jupiter's formation are still studied.
Models of Jupiter's formation help explain the structure of the Solar System.
Jupiter's composition provides evidence about conditions in the early planetary system.

## 8. INTERNAL STRUCTURE

Mercury has a large metallic core.
The core occupies a substantial fraction of Mercury's interior.
The core is surrounded by a rocky mantle.
A rocky crust forms the outermost solid layer.
Mercury's core contains a significant amount of iron.
The large core contributes to Mercury's relatively high average density.
Mercury has a global magnetic field.
The magnetic field provides evidence that at least part of the core remains active.
Scientists study Mercury's interior using spacecraft measurements and gravitational data.
Understanding Mercury's core helps explain how small terrestrial planets evolve.

## INTERNAL HEAT

Neptune emits more energy than it receives from sunlight.
The excess energy indicates that Neptune releases significant internal heat.
Internal heat can influence atmospheric circulation.
Heat from the interior may contribute to strong winds and storms.
The exact mechanism transporting internal heat remains an area of research.
Neptune's internal heat is important when comparing it with Uranus.
Both planets are ice giants with similar overall compositions.
Neptune produces substantially more internal energy than Uranus.
Differences in internal structure may help explain their different atmospheric behavior.
Studying internal heat helps scientists understand ice giant evolution.

## DWARF PLANETS AND ORBITAL DYNAMICS

Dwarf planets do not gravitationally dominate their orbital neighborhoods.
Their orbital regions contain many other small bodies.
Resonances can stabilize or modify their orbital paths.
Gravitational interactions can change orbital eccentricity and inclination.
Some dwarf planets have highly inclined or elongated orbits.
Orbital dynamics help explain the different populations of distant objects.
Long-term simulations are used to study their orbital evolution.
The gravitational influence of Neptune is particularly important beyond its orbit.
Close encounters can alter the trajectories of smaller bodies.
Orbital dynamics are central to understanding why dwarf planets differ from planets.

## ORBITAL MIGRATION

Planetary migration occurs when a planet's orbit changes after formation.
Interactions with a protoplanetary disk can alter orbital distance.
Gravitational interactions between planets can also change their orbits.
A planet can move closer to or farther from its host star.
Migration can explain planets found extremely close to their stars.
It can also influence the arrangement of multiple-planet systems.
Migration may occur during the early stages of planetary system evolution.
Resonances can develop when migrating planets interact gravitationally.
Planetary migration is an important part of modern planet-formation models.
The exact migration history of an individual exoplanet may be difficult to determine.

## ICE GIANT INTERIOR

The term ice giant refers to Uranus and Neptune.
In planetary science, "ice" includes substances such as water, ammonia, and methane.
These materials can exist in unusual high-pressure states inside a planet.
The deep interior of Uranus is extremely hot and highly compressed.
Water may become electrically conductive under extreme interior conditions.
Laboratory experiments study high-pressure water states relevant to ice giants.
Superionic water is one proposed state that may occur deep inside Uranus.
Such exotic states could help explain the planet's magnetic field.
Interior models are based on observations, physics, and computer simulations.
The exact internal structure of Uranus is not directly observable.

## 16. MAGNETIC FIELD AND ATMOSPHERIC LOSS

Mars does not currently have a strong global magnetic field like Earth.
Some regions of the Martian crust retain evidence of ancient magnetization.
This suggests Mars may have had a stronger global magnetic field early in its history.
The loss of a global magnetic field allowed the solar wind to interact more directly with the upper atmosphere.
Solar wind interactions can contribute to atmospheric escape.
Atmospheric loss is one factor in the long-term evolution of Mars.
Mars's thin present atmosphere may partly result from billions of years of atmospheric loss.
Studying atmospheric escape helps explain how Mars changed from its ancient environment to its present state.

## ASTEROIDS — OVERVIEW

Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun.
Most asteroids are much smaller than planets.
Asteroids are remnants of material left over from the formation of the Solar System.
They are classified as small Solar System bodies.
Most known asteroids are concentrated in the main asteroid belt.
The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids can have irregular, spherical, elongated, or highly fractured shapes.
Their surfaces can contain rocks, dust, impact craters, and regolith.
Asteroids vary greatly in size, composition, brightness, and orbital properties.
Studying asteroids provides information about the early Solar System.

## FORMATION

Asteroids formed from material present in the protoplanetary disk.
The protoplanetary disk surrounded the young Sun.
Small solid particles collided and gradually accumulated during Solar System formation.
Gravitational interactions influenced how these bodies grew and moved.
In the asteroid belt, Jupiter's gravity prevented many objects from forming a single planet.
Collisions repeatedly fragmented larger bodies.
Some asteroids are therefore fragments of older parent bodies.
Other asteroids may preserve relatively primitive material.
Asteroids can retain chemical information from the early Solar System.

## Their compositions help scientists investigate planetary formation.

Asteroid formation and evolution occurred over billions of years.

Looking farther into space generally means looking farther back in time.
Light requires a finite amount of time to travel between astronomical objects.

## COSMOLOGICAL DISTANCES

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.
Comoving distance accounts for cosmic expansion when describing large-scale positions.
Proper distance describes physical separation at a specified cosmic time.
Lookback time measures how long light has traveled to reach an observer.
Luminosity distance is defined using the observed brightness of an object.
Angular-diameter distance relates an object's physical size to its observed angular size.

Looking farther into space generally means looking farther back in time.
Light requires a finite amount of time to travel between astronomical objects.
A galaxy millions of light-years away is observed as it existed millions of years ago.

The cosmic microwave background comes from an even earlier period.
Astronomers use distant observations to reconstruct the history of the universe.

and planet with the light from the star alone.

This can reveal information about atmospheric temperature and composition.
Mid-infrared observations are particularly useful for studying thermal radiation.

The Big Bang model is supported by several independent observations.
These include cosmic expansion, the cosmic microwave background, and the observed abundance of light elements.
The model describes the evolution of the observable universe but does not by itself explain every question about the ultimate beginning.

## 31. JWST Versus Hubble

Hubble and JWST are complementary observatories.
Hubble operates primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared wavelengths.
JWST focuses mainly on infrared wavelengths.
Hubble has a primary mirror approximately 2.4 meters in diameter.
JWST has a segmented primary mirror approximately 6.5 meters in diameter.
JWST therefore has a significantly larger light-collecting area.
Hubble operates in low Earth orbit.
JWST operates near the Sun-Earth L2 region.
Hubble can be serviced by astronauts because of its location.
JWST was designed without routine crewed servicing.

JWST can investigate dust surrounding young stars and active galaxies.
Dust composition can also provide clues about chemical processes occurring in space.
Understanding dust is essential because dust participates in the formation of stars and
planets.

## 4. The JWST Primary Mirror

The primary mirror is one of JWST's most recognizable components.

of an idea that would eventually drive me to sell everything I owned and
buy a one-way ticket to South America.

much about time management as it is about mind management.

The model describes the evolution of the observable universe but does not by itself explain every question about the ultimate beginning.

Hubble and JWST are complementary observatories.
Hubble operates primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared wavelengths.
JWST focuses mainly on infrared wavelengths.

JWST has a segmented primary mirror approximately 6.5 meters in diameter.
JWST therefore has a significantly larger light-collecting area.
Hubble operates in low Earth orbit.

## 94. General Relativity

General relativity is Albert Einstein's theory of gravitation.

Mass and energy influence spacetime curvature.

Objects move through this curved spacetime according to the theory's equations.

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.
Comoving distance accounts for cosmic expansion when describing large-scale positions.
Proper distance describes physical separation at a specified cosmic time.
Lookback time measures how long light has traveled to reach an observer.
Luminosity distance is defined using the observed brightness of an object.
Angular-diameter distance relates an object's physical size to its observed angular size.

COSMOLOGY
Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe.
Modern cosmology combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy.
The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy.
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old according to current measurements.
The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while light was traveling.
The observable universe is the region from which light or other signals have had time to reach us.
The entire universe may be much larger than the observable universe.
Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite is not currently known.

## OBSERVATIONAL COSMOLOGY

Observational cosmology uses astronomical measurements to test models of the universe.
The cosmic microwave background is one of its most important datasets.
Type Ia supernovae are used as distance indicators for studying cosmic expansion.
Galaxy surveys measure positions, redshifts, and properties of millions of galaxies.
Baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler for measuring cosmic distances.
Weak gravitational lensing traces the distribution of matter.
Galaxy clusters provide information about structure growth and dark matter.

## 31. George Smoot

George Smoot is an American astrophysicist and cosmologist.

He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2006 with John Mather.

Their work involved measurements of the cosmic microwave background using the COBE satellite.

The cosmic microwave background is electromagnetic radiation originating from the early universe.

Smoot appeared on The Big Bang Theory as himself.

His presence connects the fictional characters to real observational cosmology.

His scientific background is particularly relevant to the show's references to the early universe and cosmology.

## 20. Dark Matter

Dark matter is a term used for matter inferred from gravitational effects that does not appear to interact strongly with electromagnetic radiation.

Astronomers have observed gravitational phenomena that cannot be fully explained by visible matter alone.

Examples include galaxy rotation and gravitational lensing.

Dark matter remains an active area of scientific research.

The exact identity of dark matter is not yet established.

The concept is frequently mentioned in discussions of cosmology and astrophysics.

Raj's scientific interests make astronomy and cosmology natural subjects for the series.

Lithium observations show some unresolved differences with simple theoretical predictions.
Big Bang nucleosynthesis is one of the major tests of early-universe cosmology.
It connects nuclear physics with the history of cosmic expansion.

LAMBDA-CDM
Lambda-CDM is the standard model of modern cosmology.
Lambda represents the cosmological constant associated with dark energy.
CDM stands for cold dark matter.
The model also includes ordinary baryonic matter and radiation.

Conditions required for generating a matter-antimatter asymmetry are studied in particle physics and cosmology.
The observed asymmetry is an important unresolved problem in fundamental physics.
Understanding baryogenesis could explain why ordinary matter exists in large quantities today.

The entire universe may be much larger than the observable universe.
Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite is not currently known.
Cosmology studies the universe on scales much larger than individual galaxies.
The standard cosmological model is commonly called Lambda-CDM.

The specific physical mechanism responsible for inflation has not been established.
Different inflationary models propose different fields and potential energy landscapes.
Inflation remains an important theoretical framework in early-universe cosmology.
Direct confirmation of a specific inflationary model has not yet been achieved.

Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe.

The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy.

## 94. General Relativity

General relativity is Albert Einstein's theory of gravitation.

It describes gravity in terms of the geometry of spacetime.

Mass and energy influence spacetime curvature.

Objects move through this curved spacetime according to the theory's equations.

General relativity predicts phenomena such as gravitational time dilation, gravitational lensing, and black holes.

The theory is frequently relevant to discussions of cosmology and astrophysics.

## COSMOLOGICAL DISTANCES

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.
Comoving distance accounts for cosmic expansion when describing large-scale positions.
Proper distance describes physical separation at a specified cosmic time.
Lookback time measures how long light has traveled to reach an observer.
Luminosity distance is defined using the observed brightness of an object.
Angular-diameter distance relates an object's physical size to its observed angular size.

## 97. Cosmological Expansion

The universe is expanding on large scales.

Galaxies generally show increasing recession velocities with increasing distance.

This relationship is described by Hubble's law in appropriate contexts.

Modern cosmology uses more precise models involving the expansion history of the universe.

The Big Bang model describes the universe evolving from an early hot, dense state.

The show occasionally references these cosmological ideas through Raj and Sheldon.

## 117. Stephen Hawking and Scientific Popular Culture

Stephen Hawking became an important figure in public discussions of cosmology and black holes.

His books introduced difficult scientific ideas to broad audiences.

His appearance on The Big Bang Theory reflects his cultural importance.

The show treats him as both a respected scientist and a participant in comedy.

His presence is an example of how real scientists can become cultural figures beyond academia.

Type Ia supernovae are used as distance indicators for studying cosmic expansion.

Weak gravitational lensing traces the distribution of matter.

## 94. General Relativity

General relativity is Albert Einstein's theory of gravitation.

It describes gravity in terms of the geometry of spacetime.

Mass and energy influence spacetime curvature.

Objects move through this curved spacetime according to the theory's equations.

General relativity predicts phenomena such as gravitational time dilation, gravitational lensing, and black holes.

The theory is frequently relevant to discussions of cosmology and astrophysics.

## COSMOLOGICAL DISTANCES

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.
Comoving distance accounts for cosmic expansion when describing large-scale positions.
Proper distance describes physical separation at a specified cosmic time.
Lookback time measures how long light has traveled to reach an observer.
Luminosity distance is defined using the observed brightness of an object.
Angular-diameter distance relates an object's physical size to its observed angular size.

## 97. Cosmological Expansion

The universe is expanding on large scales.

Galaxies generally show increasing recession velocities with increasing distance.

This relationship is described by Hubble's law in appropriate contexts.

Modern cosmology uses more precise models involving the expansion history of the universe.

The Big Bang model describes the universe evolving from an early hot, dense state.

The show occasionally references these cosmological ideas through Raj and Sheldon.

## 117. Stephen Hawking and Scientific Popular Culture

Stephen Hawking became an important figure in public discussions of cosmology and black holes.

His books introduced difficult scientific ideas to broad audiences.

His appearance on The Big Bang Theory reflects his cultural importance.

The show treats him as both a respected scientist and a participant in comedy.

His presence is an example of how real scientists can become cultural figures beyond academia.

## 94. General Relativity

General relativity is Albert Einstein's theory of gravitation.

It describes gravity in terms of the geometry of spacetime.

Mass and energy influence spacetime curvature.

Objects move through this curved spacetime according to the theory's equations.

General relativity predicts phenomena such as gravitational time dilation, gravitational lensing, and black holes.

The theory is frequently relevant to discussions of cosmology and astrophysics.

## COSMOLOGICAL DISTANCES

Cosmology uses several different definitions of distance.
Comoving distance accounts for cosmic expansion when describing large-scale positions.
Proper distance describes physical separation at a specified cosmic time.
Lookback time measures how long light has traveled to reach an observer.
Luminosity distance is defined using the observed brightness of an object.
Angular-diameter distance relates an object's physical size to its observed angular size.

## 97. Cosmological Expansion

The universe is expanding on large scales.

Galaxies generally show increasing recession velocities with increasing distance.

This relationship is described by Hubble's law in appropriate contexts.

Modern cosmology uses more precise models involving the expansion history of the universe.

The Big Bang model describes the universe evolving from an early hot, dense state.

The show occasionally references these cosmological ideas through Raj and Sheldon.

Stephen Hawking became an important figure in public discussions of cosmology and black holes.

His books introduced difficult scientific ideas to broad audiences.

His appearance on The Big Bang Theory reflects his cultural importance.

The show treats him as both a respected scientist and a participant in comedy.

His presence is an example of how real scientists can become cultural figures beyond academia.
